Bond-servant
BOND-sur-vunt
n.
A compound of Old English bond (one bound; from Old Norse bóndi, a householder, later a serf) and servant (from Old French servant, one who serves); used in English translations of the New Testament to render Greek doulos — a slave with no legal rights of his own, whose will is wholly subject to his master's. Modern translations often prefer “slave” to preserve the legal force; “bond-servant” captures the covenantal warmth of voluntary submission.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Bond-servant is the English rendering used by many translations for Greek doulos — the term by which the apostles designated themselves before Christ and by which God designates His most honoured servants across the entire biblical canon. Paul opens Romans and Philippians with the same self-identification: “Paul, a bondservant of Christ Jesus” (Rom 1:1; Phil 1:1). This is not false modesty; it is precise covenant theology. A doulos in the Greco-Roman world had no legal autonomy — his time, labour, and obedience belonged entirely to his master. Paul's adoption of the title declares that his entire apostolic existence is owned, directed, and authorised by Christ. The Revelation opens with the same framing: “The Revelation of Jesus Christ — which God gave Him to show to His bondservants the things that must shortly take place” (Rev 1:1). The bond-servant is the one to whom Christ reveals His purposes, making the title not merely one of submission but of extraordinary covenantal intimacy. The Old Testament background is the voluntary bond-servant of Exodus 21:5–6 — the slave who, at the end of his term, chooses to remain with his master out of love, has his ear pierced against the doorpost, and serves for life. This is the template: a freely chosen, love-driven subjection that the world reads as limitation but that Scripture reads as the highest honour. Paul resolves the paradox: “he who was called in the Lord while a slave is the Lord's freedman — likewise he who was called while free is Christ's slave” (1 Cor 7:22). True freedom is found in willing subjection to the One who bought us with His blood.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a bond-servant as one held in servitude; in New Testament theology the term is voluntarily adopted by the apostles as their highest self-designation, naming them as those whose entire existence belongs to Christ and whose service is their truest freedom.

expand to see more

BOND-SERVANT, n. A servant bound to service without wages; one who holds the legal status of a slave. Webster (1828) distinguishes bond-servant from hired servant: the bond-servant has no exit clause, no independent claim on his time, and no labour he can withhold from his master.

In the New Testament the term's legal severity is redeemed by its covenantal context: Christ's bond-servants are not coerced but purchased at infinite cost (1 Pet 1:18–19) and their service flows from gratitude and love. The Exodus 21 voluntary bond-servant who chooses permanent service out of love for his master is the Old Testament type that illuminates the apostolic self-designation.

Key Scripture

Romans 1:1 — "Paul, a bondservant of Christ Jesus — called as an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God,"

Philippians 1:1 — "Paul and Timothy, bondservants of Christ Jesus — to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are in Philippi, with the overseers and deacons:"

Revelation 1:1 — "The Revelation of Jesus Christ — which God gave Him to show to His bondservants the things that must shortly take place. He made it known by sending it through His angel to His bondservant John,"

1 Corinthians 7:22 — "For he who was called in the Lord while a slave is the Lord’s freedman — likewise he who was called while free is Christ’s slave."

Modern Corruption

The church-growth movement has replaced the bond-servant model with consumer-oriented “ministry leadership,” treating the pastor as a service provider and the congregation as a clientele; individualist Christianity resists the total claim of the Master, insisting on a Christianity that leaves large territories of the self un-surrendered and unexamined.

expand to see more

The managerial revolution in American evangelicalism has reframed pastoral identity around corporate leadership categories — CEOs, visionary leaders, executive directors — rather than the apostolic self-designation of bond-servant. The result is a Christianity in which the minister manages rather than submits, casts vision rather than proclaims a received word, and serves the preferences of the congregation rather than the will of the Master. The bond-servant has no vision of his own; he carries his master's message. The apostolic letters open with “bondservant,” not “visionary leader,” precisely because the authority of the apostolic message derives from the One who sent it, not from the personality of the one who delivered it.

Individualist Christianity treats the gospel as a rescue operation that delivers the self into a realm of personal autonomy — Christ saves me so I can live my best life on my own terms. The bond-servant metaphor explodes this: the one purchased by the blood of Christ is not emancipated into self-determination but into a new and glorious bondage. His time belongs to Christ. His tongue belongs to Christ. His body, mind, and strength are the Master's tools. This is not oppression; it is, as Paul insists in 1 Cor 7:22, the definition of true freedom — because the Master who owns the bond-servant is the One who died for him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Old Testament institution of the voluntary bond-servant (Exod 21:5–6) and the prophetic self-designation “servant of the LORD” provide the background for the New Testament apostolic title; Christ Himself took the form of a doulos (Phil 2:7), making bond-service the shape of the incarnation.

expand to see more

Greek doulos — slave, bond-servant; one with no legal autonomy, wholly subject to the master's will; used of Paul, Timothy, James, Peter, Jude, and the prophets.

Hebrew ʿeved — servant, slave; used of Moses (“Moses My servant,” Num 12:7), David (“David My servant,” 2 Sam 3:18), and the Suffering Servant of Isa 53.

Exodus 21:5–6 — the voluntary bond-servant who chooses permanent service out of love; the ear pierced at the doorpost as a mark of covenantal belonging; Old Testament type of apostolic bond-service.

Philippians 2:7 — Christ “took the form of a bond-servant” (morphen doulou); the Incarnation itself is framed as doulos existence, making bond-service Christomorphic.

English “bond-servant” — KJV-era compound rendering that preserves both the legal bond (involuntary dimension) and the service orientation (relational dimension) of doulos.

Usage

"The apostolic use of “bondservant of Christ Jesus” as an opening self-designation establishes the authority of the letter: this is not Paul's private opinion but the word of one whose entire existence is owned and directed by the risen Lord."

"The Old Testament volunteer bond-servant (Exod 21) who pierces his ear at the doorpost is the typological background for the apostolic title: love-driven permanent submission to a benevolent master, freely chosen at the end of a term that had already been served."

"Christ Himself “took the form of a bond-servant” (Phil 2:7) in the Incarnation, making doulos existence not a degraded station but the very shape of divine love entering human history to accomplish redemption."
